title: Computer Security Incident Handling Guide: incident response life cycle
content: The incident response life cycle has four phases: preparation; detection and analysis; containment, eradication and recovery; and post-incident activity. Preparation establishes the capability before an incident occurs, including tooling, contacts and communication plans. Detection and analysis determines whether an incident has occurred, its scope and its impact, and requires correlating evidence from several sources because a single indicator is rarely conclusive. Containment decisions balance stopping the damage against preserving evidence and maintaining service, and organisations should decide containment strategy in advance for each incident type rather than during the event. Post-incident review converts the event into improved detection and prevention.

title: Computer Security Incident Handling Guide: evidence handling and prioritisation
content: Incidents should be prioritised by functional impact, information impact and recoverability rather than handled first-in first-out. Evidence should be collected according to documented procedures with a maintained chain of custody, because containment actions frequently destroy volatile evidence. Detailed records of every action taken, with timestamps, support both the investigation and any subsequent legal process. Handlers should preserve volatile data such as memory and active network connections before shutting down or reimaging an affected system.

title: Digital Identity Guidelines: authentication and lifecycle management
content: Verifiers should compare prospective passwords against lists of values known to be commonly used or compromised, and should not impose composition rules or arbitrary periodic rotation, which drive predictable user behaviour. Rate limiting must be applied to defend against online guessing, with a limited number of consecutive failed attempts per account. Multi-factor authentication substantially reduces the value of a stolen or guessed password, and phishing-resistant authenticators offer the strongest protection against credential interception. Passwords should be salted and hashed with a memory-hard function before storage.

title: SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet
content: The primary defence against SQL injection is the use of prepared statements with parameterised queries, which keep user input as bound data that can never alter query structure. Where parameterisation is impossible, such as for dynamic table or column names, use a strict allowlist of permitted values. Secondary defences include applying least privilege to the database account and validating input, but neither replaces parameterisation. Escaping user input by hand is error prone and should be a last resort.

title: Cross Site Scripting Prevention Cheat Sheet
content: Prevent cross-site scripting by encoding untrusted data for the specific context in which it is rendered, since the rules for HTML body, attributes, JavaScript and URLs differ. Prefer frameworks that encode by default and avoid sinks that write raw markup into the document. A Content-Security-Policy provides defence in depth by restricting which scripts may execute, and HttpOnly cookies limit the value of a successful payload. Where user-supplied HTML must be permitted, sanitise it with a maintained library rather than a custom filter.

title: OWASP Top 10 Web Application Security Risks
content: The OWASP Top 10 is a consensus document describing the most critical categories of web application security risk, used widely as an awareness and baseline assurance reference. Categories include broken access control, cryptographic failures, injection, insecure design, security misconfiguration, vulnerable and outdated components, identification and authentication failures, software and data integrity failures, security logging and monitoring failures, and server-side request forgery. Injection covers SQL, command and similar defects where untrusted input is interpreted as part of a command. Logging and monitoring failures are included because undetected breaches persist far longer and cost substantially more to resolve.

title: Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks
content: Social engineering attacks manipulate a person into disclosing information or taking an action rather than exploiting a technical defect. Recipients should be suspicious of unsolicited messages that create urgency, request credentials, or ask them to follow a link to verify an account. Verifying the request through an independently known contact route, rather than the details supplied in the message, defeats most such attempts. Organisations should provide a simple mechanism for staff to report suspicious messages, since early reporting enables the whole campaign to be scoped and removed.

title: Understanding and Responding to Distributed Denial-of-Service Attacks
content: A distributed denial-of-service attack uses many sources to exhaust the capacity of a target service or its network path. Preparation matters more than reaction: organisations should understand their normal traffic profile, know their provider's mitigation options, and hold contacts ready before an event. During an attack, characterise the traffic and engage the upstream provider or a scrubbing service, because saturation of the inbound link cannot be mitigated at the far end. Rate limiting and geographic or protocol filtering can preserve capacity for legitimate users, and service degradation should be planned so that critical functions survive.

title: Guide to Malware Incident Prevention and Handling for Desktops and Laptops
content: Malware incident handling combines prevention through patching, least privilege and application restriction with detection through endpoint and network monitoring. Containment should consider the trade-off between isolating a host quickly and preserving volatile evidence needed to understand the intrusion. Identification of the specific malware and its indicators enables the estate to be searched for other affected hosts before eradication begins. Recovery should restore from known-good media or backups, because cleaning in place cannot guarantee the removal of persistence mechanisms.

title: Using ATT&CK for threat-informed analysis
content: ATT&CK is a curated knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques observed in real intrusions, organised so that tactics represent the adversary objective and techniques the means of achieving it. Mapping observed activity to techniques supports consistent communication, gap analysis of detection coverage, and reasoning about what an adversary is likely to do next. A mapping should be asserted only where the available evidence supports it; speculative mapping inflates apparent confidence and misleads later analysis. Because a single observation often fits several techniques, analysts should record the evidence that justified the chosen mapping.
